what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Personal agents converge on files; keys decide privacy
sections.para: Seven always-on personal agents, from Meta's Muse to OpenClaw, are read through the Agent Behaviour Policy and a data-sovereignty lens. Muse's separate permission authority is a real barrier, but Meta admits its memory protection is policy, not cryptography. A design follows: vaults the host cannot read, attested enclaves, per-task keys and pages people can read.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Shared shape, different barriers, vendor-held keys, open alternative
sections.para: The 2026 products share one shape: cloud computer, file memory, connectors, confirmation prompts; Muse's Sentinel is a true boundary, most others offer settings. Memory mostly sits in vendor clouds under vendor keys, and pages on non-users have no route to rights. The proposed design keeps the files but moves the keys to the user.

sections.label: The year the agent got a computer
sections.line: In 2026 every major vendor shipped an always-on agent
sections.para: Spark (19 May), Scout later Autopilot (2 June), Siri (8 June), Grok Bot (11 August), Muse (8 September) and dots (29 September) all launched in 2026. Behind them sits OpenClaw, a self-hosted gateway with a quarter of a million GitHub stars that Nat Friedman confirmed inspired Muse. Adoption ran into the millions.

sections.label: Lens one: what stops the agent
sections.line: Reach is maximised, mandates unwritten, only Sentinel bounds
sections.para: Read as behaviour policies, every product maximises reach into email, payments and messages, and none asks for a written mandate; the terms make the user liable. Meta's Sentinel is a separate permission authority and a genuine boundary, while dots, Spark, Cowork and Alexa+ offer settings. September 2026 incidents showed hijackers inherit the full reach.

sections.label: Lens two: who can read what it knows
sections.line: Vendors hold the keys, and non-users have no recourse
sections.para: Most memory rests in vendor clouds; Meta says today's Muse does not prevent Meta accessing data, with a Confidential VM still in testing. Apple's Private Cloud Compute is the strongest design. Training is often on by default, and Muse keeps a page per person that non-users cannot reach, which the ICO, CNIL and GDPR Article 25 make hard to defend.

sections.label: What pays for it, and how much to trust
sections.line: Business models make privacy promises a matter of policy
sections.para: Muse is free with $20 and $100 tiers and Zuckerberg expects transaction fees; dots come with OpenAI's paid tiers and Spark needs Google's top subscription. Many vendors live on advertising, and a page on everyone you know is a complete profile. Trust becomes a personal arithmetic the second half aims to change.

sections.label: The convergence
sections.line: Muse and the team's CRM reached the same shape
sections.para: Muse's page per person and the team's vault folder per person are the same design: files, no database, filled only from evidence. Meta's came via OpenClaw; the team's came from the vault model. So privacy is not an architecture question: what differs is who holds the keys, who reads the pages and what pays.

sections.label: A privacy-first design on this technology
sections.line: Vaults, a policy authority and attested enclaves keep secrets
sections.para: The design stores memory in client-encrypted vaults, puts a readable behaviour policy in a separate permission authority, and runs steps in the browser, then in an attested enclave, to which the user's device wraps a per-task key destroyed afterwards. People can read their own folder. Physical attacks and vendor roots remain open.

sections.label: What exists today, and what does not
sections.line: Vaults and policy exist; authority and enclave do not
sections.para: Built: client-encrypted vaults, read keys, append lanes, the behaviour policy in practice, browser decryption, and cloud confidential compute. Missing: an enforcing permission authority, a browser-checked enclave image, per-task key release, scoped vault reads, key revocation, signed authorship and cost measurements. A five-step build order is set out.

sections.label: The question underneath
sections.line: Holding the key differs from holding the information's mandate
sections.para: The design keeps secrets from host, vendor and model, but leaves open who gives the mandate over information a person gave to the user, not to an agent. That question gets its own document. Policies per agent, rules per relationship, per-task keys and showable memory are the mechanisms any answer would need.

sections.label: Sources
sections.line: Sources: vendor pages, press reports, regulators and research cited
sections.para: Sources include Meta's Muse launch, engineering post, policy and terms, Wired's 3 October 2026 report, and launch pages for dots, Spark, Scout, Siri, Cowork, Alexa+ and OpenClaw. Also AWS, Google, Microsoft and NVIDIA confidential compute docs, WireTap and TEE.fail, the ICO and CNIL notes and GDPR. Drafted by Claude from Dinis Cruz's memo.
